title: 0492-analysing-skill-predominance-in-generalized-fantasy
universal_lens: The core primitive is the "Crowding-Dilution Operator", which maps fantasy contest prize structure to reduced skill premium. It arises from shared pooling, where adding more correct picks merely splits the fixed prize, lowering expected returns. This mirrors NFL DFS ownership equilibrium, where popular plays reduce optimizer edge through increased competition for prizes. Both settings exhibit diminishing marginal utility of skill due to resource sharing.
gsi_mapping: In GSI, this maps to a "Bayesian Ownership Correction" framework. Observing that multiple bettors select the same side (crowding) reduces the posterior probability that the consensus play is mispriced. The primitive adjusts the conformal prediction interval for the bettor's edge, shrinking it proportionally to the inverse of the number of other bettors taking the same action. This prevents overbetting on crowded edges and aligns with GSI's goal of robust statistical arbitrage.
gse_mapping: In GSE, the primitive manifests as a "State-Transition Damping Mechanism". When a quarterback throws to a crowded receiver (high ownership), the expected utility of the pass decreases because defenders can anticipate and double-team. The state-transition matrix incorporates a decay factor that penalizes actions with high historical co-selection frequencies, effectively simulating the dilution effect. This guides the model toward less congested passing lanes, improving situational efficiency.

primitives.name: Crowding-Dilution Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: # [0492] Analysing Skill Predominance in Generalized Fantasy Cricket (arXiv:2512.18467v1) **Citation:** Supratim Das, Sarthak Sarkar, Subhamoy Maitra, Tridib Mukherjee (2026).
primitives.assumptions: Shared prize pool, equicorrelated log-normal team scores, analytical players with noisy Dirichlet belief updates, IID lowest-contributor shares.
primitives.breakdown_regime: As the number of analytical players approaches zero or the correlation between team performances tends to one, the operator becomes singular because either there is no competition for the prize or all teams become perfectly indistinguishable.

layer2.mapping: Maps to NFL DFS ownership equilibrium models where increased selection frequency of a high-edge lineup reduces its expected value due to prize pool fragmentation. Both settings involve resource-sharing mechanisms that diminish the marginal benefit of superior information.
layer2.telemetry: Measured as the ratio of mean winnings for an optimal strategy versus a random baseline, varying the fraction of analytical players and the number of expert teams.

primitives.name: Dirichlet Belief Update
primitives.verbatim_quote: (b) Player behavior: analytical players sample beliefs p∼Dirichlet(απ) with concentration α calibrated so p is within β of π with probability ≥1-δ, via Chebyshev + union bound: α≥n/(4δβ2)-1 (Appendix A); then team choice ∼Multinomial(1,p).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'p_i': 'Probability of selecting team i, dimensionless', 'π_i': 'True win probability of team i, dimensionless', 'α': 'Concentration parameter of Dirichlet distribution, dimensionless', 'β': 'Maximum acceptable error in belief estimate, dimensionless', 'δ': 'Upper bound on failure probability, dimensionless', 'n': 'Number of teams, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: Analytical players have access to true win probabilities π_i; beliefs are updated using a conjugate Dirichlet prior with parameter α times the true probabilities; the update is Bayes-optimal given the squared loss.
primitives.breakdown_regime: As α approaches zero, the posterior distribution collapses to a point mass at the prior mean π_i, rendering the update ineffective. Conversely, as α grows large, the posterior tightly concentrates around the empirical frequencies, ignoring the prior.

layer2.mapping: Maps to Bayesian updating in NFL betting markets where oddsmakers combine prior beliefs (implied probabilities) with new data (sharp money flows) using a Dirichlet-multinomial likelihood. The concentration parameter α reflects the perceived reliability of the prior.
layer2.telemetry: Tracking the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the posterior Dirichlet distribution and the true underlying win probability vector across repeated trials.

primitives.name: Ownership Equilibrium Correction
primitives.verbatim_quote: (e) Extensions: number of experts ∈{2,3,4}; correlation ρ∈{0.1,...,0.9}; Impact Player: 4 candidate impact players (I_1,...,I_4)∼LogNormal(μ_I,Σ_I), ρ_I=0.3, independent of P; lowest-contributor share S_i∼DirichletMin(α) (minimum coordinate of Dirichlet(α), α=10·1 over 11 players); boosted score B_ij=P_i(1-S_i)+max(S_i·P_i, I_j); contest over team–impact-player combos.
primitives.assumptions: Fixed prize pool shared among winners; team selection follows either analytical or random strategies; lowest-contributor shares are IID across teams.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When all players adopt the same strategy (all analytical or all random), the selection ratio is undefined. Additionally, if the prize pool is zero (no winners), the mean winnings metric becomes trivially zero.

layer2.mapping: Maps to the adjustment made in NFL DFS when calculating the expected value of a lineup. The correction accounts for the fact that high-ownership lineups are more likely to be shared with other winning entries, thereby reducing the individual payout even if the lineup wins.
layer2.telemetry: Observing the correlation between the percentage of entries using a particular player and the realized return on investment (ROI) for those entries across multiple tournaments.

reasoning_traces.think:
The Crowding-Dilution Operator (CDO) emerges from the tension between information asymmetry and resource scarcity. In a fantasy cricket contest, an analytical player possesses superior knowledge about team performance (skill). However, when multiple such players converge on the 'best' team, they fragment the fixed prize pool, reducing each winner's payout. Mathematically, this is captured by the selection ratio metric, which compares the uptake of an optimal team versus a random one. As the number of analytical players increases, this ratio drops, leading to a "winner's curse" where the most informed participants collectively underperform. This phenomenon parallels NFL DFS ownership equilibrium: a high-edge quarterback play attracts numerous lineups, increasing the likelihood of shared first-place prizes and lowering the expected ROI for any single entry. Both systems suffer from a breakdown in the simple linear relationship between skill and reward, replaced by a nonlinear saturation function driven by market depth. The CDO thus provides a universal framework for understanding why perfect information does not guarantee proportional gains in pooled-benefit games.

reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Modeling opponents as heterogeneous mixtures of analytical and random agents reveals that the optimal strategy depends on estimating the fraction of informed participants. If a bettor assumes all others are random, they may overestimate their edge. Conversely, if they assume everyone is analytical, they may underestimate the noise. The CDO captures the strategic interaction: a player's expected utility is maximized by considering not just their own signal, but also the implicit signals embedded in the observed selection frequencies. This requires "higher-order" reasoning about the distribution of distributions.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: To avoid anti-collinearity, the model must distinguish between genuine skill-based selection and spurious patterns caused by external factors (weather, stadium effects). Leakage is prevented by ensuring that the belief-updating process uses only publicly available information (e.g., career stats) and not private signals (insider knowledge). Additionally, the equicorrelation assumption must be tested against empirical data; if team performances are conditionally independent given latent factors, the CDO's predictions will be biased.
